```json
{
  "problems": [
    "shapeGrammar: 'build every form from circle, square and triangle only' contradicts the next rule, which uses thick bars. Bars are rectangles, not squares.",
    "shapeGrammar: 'set type flush left' ignores right-to-left Arabic. Many users are from the Gulf, and Arabic must align right, to its reading start.",
    "dos: 'stay visible and honest' is a slogan, not a design instruction.",
    "dos: 'keep color flat and limited to the primaries with black and paper' leaves out the steel grey support color in the palette.",
    "dos: 'set Arabic and Latin text with the same plain, built logic' is vague. It needs concrete direction on alignment, typeface voice and real readable words."
  ],
  "fix": {
    "shapeGrammar": [
      "build every form from circle, square, triangle and straight bar only",
      "place blocks asymmetrically on a visible grid, never centered by default",
      "use thick black bars and rules as structure, not as decoration",
      "keep one large shape against several small ones to set a clear scale contrast",
      "show construction lines, guides and arcs where they explain the layout",
      "set type in sans serif aligned to its reading start, flush left for Latin and flush right for Arabic, sometimes turned 90 degrees along a bar for short labels only"
    ],
    "dos": [
      "credit the Bauhaus school and its workshops in the project notes",
      "keep grid lines, guides and arcs visible as thin steel grey rules where they explain the layout",
      "keep color flat: paper and black as the base, red, blue and yellow as accents, grey only for rules and quiet text",
      "use scale contrast to lead the eye to one main action",
      "set Arabic in a geometric Kufi or sans on the same grid and spacing as Latin, aligned right, with real readable words chosen with the user"
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
{
 "problems": [
  "story: 'listed by UNESCO as a unique example of the Najdi architectural and decorative style' reads as a quote from the listing that cannot be confirmed. Replaced with the plain fact: At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2010 and represents the Najdi architectural style.",
  "story: the sentence says crenellated rooflines keep the rooms cool. The thick walls and small high openings do that. Rewritten so each feature has its own job.",
  "story: the site name was spelled 'At-Turaif in Diriyah' here and 'At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah' in the credit. It now uses the UNESCO name in both places.",
  "donts: the line says the national emblem and the flag both carry the shahada. Only the Saudi flag carries the shahada; the national emblem of a palm and two swords does not. Split into accurate wording.",
  "donts: 'no real heritage site or real door used as a logo' is narrower than the rule. No real door, facade or site may be traced or copied at all, not just as a logo."
 ],
 "fix": {
  "story": "Najdi architecture is the mud brick building tradition of central Arabia, shaped by the builders and families of Najd. Its houses use thick earth walls and small high openings that keep the rooms cool, rows of small triangular openings that let in air and light, and stepped crenellations that finish the top of the walls. At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah, inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage site in 2010, represents this Najdi architectural style. The tradition stands for shelter made from local earth, where plain heavy mass carries a few precise cuts and painted wooden doors. On a screen this becomes calm solid blocks, sharp small geometry at the edges and a clear line between what is wall and what is opening.",
  "donts": [
   "no sacred or Quranic text as decoration",
   "no Saudi flag, which carries the shahada, as texture or pattern",
   "no national emblem as texture, pattern or decoration",
   "no tracing or copying a real door, facade or heritage site, and no real one used as a logo",
   "no hint that At-Turaif or any heritage body endorses the product",
   "no camels, dunes, palm trees, lanterns or generic arabesque as shorthand",
   "no fake script or real letters used as random pattern",
   "no mixing in Levantine, Maghrebi, Turkish or Iranian tile work"
  ]
 }
}
```

```json
{
  "problems": [
    "story: says 'Islamic architecture and calligraphy' and 'for a long time', which is the vague naming rule 2 forbids. It does not name where the square brick form grew (Iran and Central Asia) or where the name Kufic comes from (Kufa, Iraq).",
    "story: it names no example of the sacred words the form often carries, and it does not say which tier applies. The lens is filed as region gulf, which the story must correct so it does not suggest a Gulf origin (rule 7). The region field itself is outside the editable fields.",
    "credit: 'calligraphic tradition of the Islamic world' and 'its calligraphers, tile makers and builders' are generic. They do not name the region or the people who shaped the form.",
    "dos: 'credit Square Kufic and its makers' repeats the generic credit. It should name the makers and say where the credit appears.",
    "donts: 'do not present the tradition as belonging to the Gulf alone' is a slogan, not a concrete design instruction."
  ],
  "fix": {
    "story": "Square Kufic builds Arabic letters from straight strokes on a square grid, so a word reads as geometry. Kufic takes its name from the city of Kufa in Iraq. The square form grew in brick and glazed tile, a technique known in Persian as banna'i, on mosques, shrines and madrasas in Iran and Central Asia, notably under the Timurids in the 14th and 15th centuries. From there it spread across many Muslim lands, so it is not a Gulf tradition alone. It often carries sacred words, such as the names of God, the Prophet Muhammad and Ali, and the shahada. The script itself is open to use with care, but those words are sacred and never decoration, so in this lens what a block says matters as much as how it looks. A screen is already a grid of square pixels, and Square Kufic's even strokes, right angles and filled squares fit that grid well. That makes it a strong fit for wordmarks, section titles and quiet grid details.",
    "credit": "Square Kufic, the geometric Kufic script built in brick and glazed tile, shaped by the calligraphers, brick masons and tile makers of Iran, Central Asia and the wider Muslim world. Name it as Square Kufic, and have every word reviewed by a calligrapher or Arabic typographer and a native Arabic speaker.",
    "dos": [
      "set only real words the user picks, built on the square grid",
      "have a calligrapher or Arabic typographer and a native speaker check every word",
      "use the grid and right-angle strokes alone for loaders, empty states and card corners",
      "snap every stroke, gap and block edge to whole modules",
      "put a caption crediting Square Kufic and the calligraphers, brick masons and tile makers of Iran and Central Asia wherever the lens is shown"
    ],
    "donts": [
      "no sacred or Quranic text as decoration",
      "no names of God, the shahada or verses as pattern, texture or background",
      "no fake or random letters used as a pattern",
      "no sacred text on buttons, icons or anything people tap or throw away",
      "no diagonals, curves or uneven stroke widths inside the grid",
      "no lanterns, domes or generic arabesque to signal the region",
      "do not caption or label it as a Gulf or Saudi tradition; name Iran and Central Asia where its brick form grew"
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
  "problems": [
    "dos: 'use the motif tile as quiet texture behind formal moments' turns calligraphic strokes into background pattern. A lettering-free tile made of Diwani-like strokes reads as fake script to Arabic readers, which breaks rule 6 and the lens's own don'ts.",

The grammar needs to say how those qualities become page layout and abstract rules, and keep letter-like strokes for real words only.",
    "rhythm: it spaces 'strokes', which again points the motif toward imitation lettering. It should describe how blocks and rules sit in the cluster and the margin.",
    "credit: it names only today's calligraphers in the Arab world. It leaves out the Ottoman chancery scribes who shaped the style and Turkey, where it began and is still practised.",
    "donts: Diwani is tied to state documents, so the protected tier needs a concrete line against mock tughras, official seals and government decree headers."
  ],
  "fix": {
    "credit": "Diwani calligraphy is the cursive hand shaped by the scribes of the Ottoman court chancery, kept alive by the calligraphers who practise it in Turkey and across the Arab world, including the Gulf.",
    "shapeGrammar": [
      "text blocks and headings slant and rise toward the left end of the line",
      "elements stack and overlap into one tight diagonal cluster",
      "long sweeping lines carry the eye, small marks stay rare",
      "heavy and hairline rules alternate inside the same cluster",
      "the motif uses only rising bands and plain rules, never shapes that look like letter strokes",
      "generous empty margin around one dense block"
    ],
    "rhythm": "One dense, slanted cluster sits in wide calm space. Inside the cluster, blocks and rules sit close, with gaps about half the weight of the heaviest line.",
    "dos": [
      "let headings and key blocks rise on a gentle slant",
      "cluster related items tightly, then give the cluster wide margins",
      "for texture behind formal moments, use rising bands and heavy and hairline rules, not letter-like strokes",
      "keep gold and red ink for small accents on cream paper",
      "set real Arabic words with the user and a calligrapher"
    ],
    "donts": [
      "no sacred or Quranic text as decoration",
      "no letters in the motif, real or invented",
      "no fake script or script used as random pattern",
      "no passing off a font as hand-written Diwani",
      "no mock tughras, official seals or government decree headers",
      "no closed or paired arcs that read as faces",
      "no camels, dunes, lanterns or generic arabesque as shorthand"
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
 "problems": [
  "story: rule 2 asks for the medium, and the story never says what the style was made in. Add posters, books and signs.",
  "shapeGrammar: 'text flush left, ragged right' is only right for Latin. GoBanana sets Arabic for Gulf users, and Arabic reads right to left, so it must sit flush right with a ragged left edge.",
  "shapeGrammar: 'one sans serif family' clashes with the type pairs, which put a Latin family and an Arabic family side by side. It should read one family per script.",
  "dos: 'set text flush left with a ragged right edge' has the same right to left problem for Arabic text.",
  "dos: 'use one type family' clashes with the bilingual type pairs. It should read one family per script."
 ],
 "fix": {
  "story": "The Swiss or International Typographic Style is a way of setting information on a strict grid, with one sans serif family, text aligned to one edge and a lot of white space. It grew out of the posters, books and signs made by designers and teachers in Switzerland, mainly in Zurich and Basel, in the 1950s and 1960s, and spread from there to studios around the world. It stands for clarity: the layout steps back so that the information leads. It suits a screen because screens are already grids, and dashboards, tables and forms read faster when every item sits on a visible column and baseline.",
  "shapeGrammar": [
   "every item sits on a visible column and a shared baseline",
   "one sans serif family per script, hierarchy from size and weight only",
   "text aligned to the reading edge, left for Latin and right for Arabic, ragged on the other side, never centered",
   "asymmetric layout with large fields of empty space",
   "one solid color block or rule as the only accent",
   "sharp rectangles, no rounded corners, no shadows"
  ],
  "dos": [
   "show the grid: align every block to a column and the baseline",
   "use one type family per script and build hierarchy with size and weight",
   "align text to its reading edge, flush left for Latin and flush right for Arabic, with the other edge ragged",
   "mirror the asymmetric layout for Arabic pages so the heavy column sits on the reading side",
   "leave whole columns empty so the content can breathe",
   "keep red for one key action or figure per view",
   "ask the brand owner if this calm, factual look fits the product"
  ]
 }
}
```

```json
{
  "problems": [
    "story: it never names the mediums where ma is documented (architecture, garden design, Noh theatre, music), and 'designers, artists and makers' is too vague to name the people who carry it",
    "credit: 'designers and makers' is generic; the credit should name the Japanese practitioners the story credits",
    "dos: 'slow, short fades' contradicts itself and gives no usable timing",
    "donts: 'do not treat empty space as leftover room' is a slogan, not a design instruction"
  ],
  "fix": {
    "story": "Ma is the Japanese idea of the interval: the pause or empty space between things, treated as part of the design and not as leftover room. It is documented across Japanese architecture, garden design, Noh theatre and traditional music, where Japanese architects, garden makers, performers and musicians shape the gap as carefully as the thing beside it. It stands for attention and timing: the space around an element is what gives that element its weight. On a crowded screen, ma lets one thing speak at a time, which suits hero sections, onboarding steps, empty states and confirmation screens.",
    "credit": "This lens draws on ma, the Japanese idea of the meaningful interval, and credits the Japanese people who carry it, among them architects, garden makers, Noh performers and musicians. It borrows the idea of the interval only, never an artwork, a religious symbol or Japanese script.",
    "dos": [
      "let one element carry each screen",
      "give the empty space a job: lead the eye to the focus",
      "balance a small element against a wide open field, off center",
      "fade elements in over 300 to 500 ms, then hold a short pause before the next step appears",
      "use real Japanese text only if chosen with a speaker and checked by a reader",
      "credit ma as a Japanese idea in the lens notes"
    ],
    "donts": [
      "no sacred or Quranic text as decoration",
      "no temple, shrine or religious symbols as decoration",
      "no Japanese characters as pattern or texture, and no fake script",
      "no tourist cliches like cherry blossoms, torii gates, Mount Fuji or brush lettering faked to look Japanese",
      "no red circle on white or any flag or emblem shape",
      "do not fill the gaps with filler cards, badges or ads",
      "do not shrink margins or gaps to fit more content; keep the empty field at two thirds of the view or more"
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "problems": [
    "story: says printers carve the blocks; carving is usually done by specialist block carvers, and the printers stamp the cloth",
    "story: says the colors 'never' sit perfectly on top of each other, which overstates it; skilled printers register closely, and small shifts are a trace of the hand, not a rule",
    "story: does not name the people who make the cloth; the hand block printers of Sanganer and Bagru are largely from the Chhipa community",
    "credit: says the printers carve the blocks, which repeats the same factual error, and 'printer communities' is close to a generic credit; it should name the Chhipa printers and the block carvers",
    "dos: the credit instruction should name the Chhipa printers and the block carvers, matching the credit"
  ],
  "fix": {
    "story": "Hand block printing is a textile craft of India, with well-known centres in Rajasthan such as Sanganer and Bagru, where much of the printing is done by families of the Chhipa community. Carvers cut a small motif into a wooden block, and printers stamp it onto cloth by hand, again and again, in a steady repeat. Each color has its own block, so a design is built up in layers, and small shifts between the layers show the hand that printed it. The result is order made by hand: a strict grid that still shows the person who printed it. That balance of system and small human variation suits a screen, where a tight layout can feel warm instead of cold.",
    "credit": "This lens draws on the hand block printing tradition of India and credits the Chhipa printers of Sanganer and Bagru in Rajasthan, who stamp and dye this cloth, and the block carvers who cut the wooden blocks they print with.",
    "dos": [
      "build patterns from one small motif in a strict grid or half-drop",
      "give each color its own layer and offset it slightly",
      "use natural dye tones on an unbleached cotton surface",
      "draw your own simple motifs that follow the grammar",
      "credit the Chhipa printers of Sanganer and Bagru and the block carvers in the project notes",
      "keep the pattern behind content, never fighting the text"
    ]
  }
}
```
